description: Solo team led by a BS Mechanical Engineering student at TIP Quezon City (roster closed). Building Ignimetheus, an offline, browser-based flame-spread simulator for testing NASA’s fire-screening assumptions. Replay NASA Saffire flight conditions and see the model’s error against published spread rates (fitted vs held-out labelled), map where 0g and 1g margins differ, and ask a local Telemetry Assistant to explain the run. A screening and teaching tool, not validated for design.
summary:
Ignimetheus is an offline, browser-based flame-spread simulator for exploring how oxygen, flow, pressure and gravity affect fires in spacecraft. It addresses the Flame in Freefall challenge by letting anyone test a question NASA's Saffire flights were built to answer: do Earth-based flammability screening results carry over to microgravity?

A reduced-order model drives a live duct simulation with virtual thermocouples and probes, a 0g vs 1g comparison, and modeled mitigations (flame arrestor, N2 dilution). Its spread rate is fitted on two NASA Saffire cotton-fiberglass runs and checked on two held-out runs, with errors of about -12% and -13% reported openly, along with the cases it gets wrong. A local Telemetry Assistant explains each run: the solver computes every number, the language model only phrases it, and each figure is checked against the live solver state.

Ignimetheus runs with no install, no cloud and no account, so students and educators can explore microgravity fire safety anywhere, even offline. It is a screening and teaching tool, not validated for spacecraft design or certification.
details:
What it does: Ignimetheus is an offline, browser-based flame-spread simulator for spacecraft fires. A reduced-order model drives a live duct simulation with virtual thermocouples and probes, a 0g vs 1g comparison, and modeled mitigations (flame arrestor, N2 dilution). A local Telemetry Assistant explains each run.

How it compares with NASA data: One spread factor is fitted on two NASA Saffire cotton-fiberglass runs (Urban et al., 2017, NTRS 20180005168) and checked on two held-out runs: -11.7% and -12.8%. We report the misses too: the Nomex and silicone no-spread cases are calibration-informed, and the BASS-II rod reference is adapted and unverified.

Creativity and safeguards: The solver computes every figure; the language model only phrases it. A router declines unmodeled topics, a deterministic fast path handles value and probe questions, and a numeric audit rejects figures that don't match the live solver state.

Impact: Students and educators can explore where oxygen and ventilation margins shift, offline, with no install or account. A screening and teaching tool, not validated for design or certification.

Tools: TypeScript, React, Vite, Canvas, Web Workers, PWA, @mlc-ai/web-llm (Qwen3-0.6B, Qwen2.5-1.5B).

AI assistance: Code and text were drafted with AI assistants (Gemini, Claude) under the author's direction; the author ran tests and checked results against NASA sources. Early AI-drafted reference data was replaced or relabelled against NASA's published table. Local Qwen models phrase explanations; every figure comes from the solver.
